claims.text: kubeadm provides kubeadm init and kubeadm join for creating clusters; kubeadm init bootstraps a control-plane node and kubeadm join adds further nodes.

claims.text: By design kubeadm cares only about bootstrapping, not about provisioning machines; it will not install or manage the kubelet, and a container runtime must be running on the hosts before it is used; until kubeadm configures it, the installed kubelet restarts in a crashloop.

claims.text: kubeadm installs no Pod network: a CNI-based Pod network add-on must be deployed separately, and without a CNI plugin nodes stay NotReady.

claims.text: kubeadm init generates self-signed CAs in /etc/kubernetes/pki by default and signs component certificates; most sit in pki, while the scheduler's and controller-manager's (and kubelet's) client certificates go into kubeconfig files in /etc/kubernetes.
kubeadm init writes static Pod manifests for the API server, controller-manager, scheduler and (without external etcd) etcd to /etc/kubernetes/manifests, which the kubelet watches for Pods to create.
Static Pods are managed directly by the kubelet on a specific node without the API server observing them; the kubelet supervises and restarts them. Their main use is running the control plane.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io Concepts > Workloads > Pods 'Static Pods' (refs .../concepts/workloads/pods/_index.md lines 413-424)

claims.text: The kubelet creates a mirror Pod on the API server for each static Pod, named with the node hostname appended after a hyphen; no Deployment creates the control-plane Pods.
kube-controller-manager is the control-plane component that runs the built-in controllers (control loops).
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io Concepts > Overview > Kubernetes Components > kube-controller-manager

claims.text: /etc/kubernetes/pki holds three CAs: ca (cluster), etcd/ca (all etcd functions), front-proxy-ca (front-end proxy for API aggregation); apiserver.crt is the API server's serving cert, apiserver-etcd-client.crt its client cert to etcd; sa.key/sa.pub are a key pair, not a cert.

claims.text: etcd checks client and peer certificates against etcd/ca (its --trusted-ca-file and --peer-trusted-ca-file); a certificate signed by ca, such as the one in admin.conf, does not pass that check.
claims.source_hint: PKI certificates and requirements, certificate paths table line 173

claims.text: By default kubeadm signs certificates valid for one year (certificateValidityPeriod 8760h) and CAs valid for ten years (caCertificateValidityPeriod 87600h).

kubeadm certs check-expiration lists each certificate and CA with expiry and residual time (days for certificates, e.g. 364d; years for CAs, e.g. 9y), including certificates embedded in kubeconfig files such as admin.conf.

By default, a kubeadm upgrade renews the certificates kubeadm manages on each node it upgrades (opt out with --certificate-renewal=false), so a cluster whose control-plane nodes are upgraded less than a year apart does not reach the date.

kubeadm.sh only reads: docker exec into donhang-control-plane (node helper, line 8), show from scripts/lib/network-lessons.sh, builds donhang first if missing, and grep -v drops lines starting [check-expiration].

Some Kubernetes distributions for small machines bundle runtime, control-plane components and a network plugin into one install; when machines are small and the team wants fewer steps they can suit, at the cost of choosing each part.

claims.text: A container runtime is the software on a node responsible for running containers; the kubelet asks it to start and stop them (through the CRI). kind's nodes use containerd.
